Pierced
PEERST
v. (past part.)
From Old French percer, to bore through. Webster 1828: penetrated; entered by force; transfixed. In Scripture it is the word of the crucifixion prophesied a thousand years and five hundred years before it happened, and the word John chose to prove that the prophecy had been kept in the flesh.

Biblical Definition

Pierced is the crucifixion word. David wrote it in the psalm of the cross, centuries before the Romans invented the punishment: For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet (Psalm 22:16). Zechariah put it in the mouth of the LORD Himself, in the first person, and joined it to a promise of repentance: they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourneth for his only son (Zechariah 12:10). John, standing at the cross and watching a soldier open the side of Jesus with a spear, records that he saw it and bore record that ye might believe, and then cites the prophet: They shall look on him whom they pierced (John 19:37). The pronouns in Zechariah are the ones the Socinian and the modern liberal cannot handle — they shall look upon me, and then they shall mourn for him — God pierced, and the pierced One mourned for as another Person. Paul takes the same verb for a self-inflicted wound: those who covet after money have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows (1 Timothy 6:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines PIERCE as to thrust into with a pointed instrument; to penetrate; to enter; and figuratively, to affect deeply, as to pierce the heart with grief. Both the literal and the affective senses are at work in Zechariah 12:10 and Luke 2:35.

expand to see more

PIERCE, v.t. — To thrust into with a pointed instrument; to penetrate; to stab.

To enter; to force a way into; as, the shot pierced the wall.

To affect deeply; to penetrate the heart with grief or with conviction; as, a sword shall pierce through thy own soul also (Luke 2:35).

PIERCED, pp. — Penetrated; transfixed; deeply affected.

The word of Acts 2:37, they were pricked in their heart, renders a different Greek verb but the same figure — the word of God entering like a point.

Key Scripture

Psalm 22:16 — "For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet."

Zechariah 12:10 — "And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplications: and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourneth for his only son, and shall be in bitterness for him, as one that is in bitterness for his firstborn."

John 19:37 — "And again another scripture saith, They shall look on him whom they pierced."

Isaiah 53:5 — "But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed."

1 Timothy 6:10 — "For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows."

Modern Corruption

Psalm 22:16 is the most contested verse in Old Testament textual history, and the modern habit of dismissing the Christian reading as a pious alteration misstates the evidence and misses what the psalm as a whole is doing.

expand to see more

The Masoretic tradition at Psalm 22:16 reads a form usually rendered like a lion; the Septuagint, translated by Jews centuries before Christ, reads a verb meaning they pierced, and the Syriac and other ancient witnesses agree. A Hebrew manuscript from Nahal Hever supports the verbal reading as well. The Authorized Version follows the older and better-attested tradition, and the psalm around it settles the matter for any honest reader: bones out of joint, the tongue cleaving to the jaws, garments parted and lots cast for the vesture, and the cry with which our Lord opened the whole psalm from the cross. Whatever one concludes about the consonants, this is a description of a crucifixion written by a man who had never seen one.

Zechariah 12:10 is the harder text for anti-Trinitarian readings, and it should be pressed. The speaker who pours out the spirit of grace and supplications is the LORD, and He says they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and in the next clause the mourning is for him. One divine speaker, pierced, and mourned for as a distinct Person. John quotes it of the spear-thrust and Revelation 1:7 quotes it of the second advent. The doctrine of the Trinity is not a later imposition upon the Hebrew Scriptures; the Hebrew Scriptures contain sentences that cannot be construed without it, and this is one of them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew karah or ka’ari at Psalm 22:16, and daqar (H1856), to pierce or thrust through, at Zechariah 12:10; Greek ekkenteo (G1574) in John 19:37 and Revelation 1:7.

expand to see more

Hebrew daqar (H1856) — to pierce, to thrust through; Zechariah 12:10, and of the fatal thrust in 1 Samuel 31:4.

Greek ekkenteo (G1574) — to pierce, to prick out; John 19:37 and Revelation 1:7, both quoting Zechariah.

Greek nusso (G3572) — to prick, to pierce; the soldier’s spear in John 19:34.

Greek peripeiro (G4044) — to pierce through, to impale on a spit; pierced themselves through with many sorrows (1 Timothy 6:10).

Greek rhomphaia (G4501) — a large broadsword; the sword Simeon said would pierce Mary’s own soul (Luke 2:35).

Usage

"They pierced my hands and my feet (Psalm 22:16) — a crucifixion described a thousand years before the Romans devised it."

"They shall look upon me whom they have pierced (Zechariah 12:10) — the LORD speaking of His own piercing."

"Pierced themselves through with many sorrows (1 Timothy 6:10) — the self-inflicted wound of covetousness."
